blocks.content: Every Docker image is not one solid block, it is a stack of read-only layers, each one corresponding to an instruction in the Dockerfile that built it. Understanding layers is the key to understanding image size, build speed, and caching.

When Docker builds an image, most Dockerfile instructions (RUN, COPY, ADD) each produce their own layer, stacked on top of the one before it. A Dockerfile with a base image, a dependency install step, and a code copy step produces at least three stacked layers.

blocks.alt: Each instruction becomes its own stacked layer

blocks.content: If two different images both start with FROM node:18, Docker only needs to store that base layer once on disk, both images simply reference the same underlying layer data. This sharing is a major reason containerized systems are disk-efficient even when running many similar images.

blocks.alt: Identical layers are stored once, referenced by many images

blocks.content: Every layer that makes up the image itself is permanently read-only. Only when you actually run a container does Docker add one additional writable layer on top, any file changes the running container makes happen there, never touching the image's own layers underneath.

blocks.alt: Only the container adds a writable layer, the image never changes

blocks.content: 4. The Union Filesystem Ties It Together
blocks.text: 4. The Union Filesystem Ties It Together

blocks.content: You do not see separate folders for each layer when you look inside a container, you see one coherent filesystem. That illusion is created by a union filesystem (commonly OverlayFS on Linux), which merges every layer into a single unified view, with higher layers able to override files from lower ones.

blocks.alt: Many separate layers, merged into one filesystem view

blocks.content: 5. Every Layer Has Its Own Identity
blocks.text: 5. Every Layer Has Its Own Identity

blocks.content: Just like the image as a whole, each individual layer has its own content hash. This hash is exactly what Docker's build cache checks against to decide whether it can reuse a layer from a previous build instead of rebuilding it from scratch, the subject of the Image Caching topic later in this module.

blocks.alt: Each layer is independently hashed and cacheable

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: An image is a stack of read-only layers, one per Dockerfile instruction, merged into a single view by a union filesystem.
Shared base layers between images save disk space, and each layer's own content hash is what makes Docker's build cache possible.
